title: Kustomize: One Base, Many Environments
intro: The same application runs in dev, staging, and production with small differences: replica count, image tag, a hostname. Copying the manifests three times guarantees they drift apart. Kustomize keeps one base and describes each environment as a patch on top, with no templating language, and it's built into kubectl. The repository has base/ and overlays/dev, overlays/prod.

steps.prompt: Render the production overlay to the terminal without applying anything.
steps.fake_output:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    env: prod
  name: shop
  namespace: shop-prod
spec:
  replicas: 6
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: registry.example.com/shop:1.8.2
        name: shop
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: 1Gi
steps.explanation: The base Deployment with production's namespace, label, replica count, image tag, and memory limit applied.
steps.why: Rendering first shows exactly what will be sent to the cluster: plain YAML, with nothing hidden. That's Kustomize's main difference from Helm: there are no templates to evaluate in your head, only patches over valid manifests. 'kubectl kustomize' uses the version built into kubectl, which lags the standalone 'kustomize' binary; pick one and use it in CI too.

steps.prompt: See what applying the production overlay would change in the live cluster.
steps.fake_output:
--- live
+++ merged
@@ spec.template.spec.containers[0] @@
-        image: registry.example.com/shop:1.8.1
+        image: registry.example.com/shop:1.8.2
steps.explanation: One line would change: the image tag.
steps.why: -k tells kubectl to build the directory with Kustomize first. Diffing against the live cluster catches what rendering alone can't: a field someone changed by hand, or a much bigger change than the pull request suggested. Make it a required step before any production apply.

steps.explanation: The rendered manifests were applied in one step.
steps.why: In a GitOps setup you wouldn't run this by hand: Argo CD or Flux builds the overlay and applies it when the repository changes. Both understand Kustomize natively, which is one reason it's the common choice for environment configuration.

steps.prompt: CI has built a new image. From inside overlays/prod, set the image named shop to registry.example.com/shop:1.8.3 in the kustomization file.
steps.fake_output:
(no output: kustomization.yaml updated)

images:
- name: shop
  newName: registry.example.com/shop
  newTag: 1.8.3
steps.explanation: The overlay's images section now pins the new tag.
steps.why: This is how a pipeline promotes a build: it changes one line in the overlay and commits it, and Git records who deployed what and when. The base manifest is never edited. Pin a digest ('newName@sha256:...') instead of a tag when you need the exact bytes guaranteed.

steps.prompt:
A base ConfigMap is created with configMapGenerator, which adds a hash to its name (app-config-7g2k9d4c5t). Why is that hash useful?
  a) It makes the name harder to guess
  b) A changed config gets a new name, which changes the Deployment's pod template, so pods roll out automatically with the new config
  c) It encrypts the data
  d) It saves etcd space
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
config changed -> ConfigMap app-config-m9t4h2f8kc (new name)
               -> Deployment now references the new name
               -> pod template changed -> rolling update
steps.hint: Normally, editing a ConfigMap doesn't restart the pods that use it.
steps.explanation: The hash turns a config change into a rollout.
steps.why: A plain ConfigMap edited in place reaches no running pod until something restarts it, which is the same trap as a rotated Secret. Generated names fix it, and they make rollback complete as well: reverting the commit brings back the old config and the old pods together. Old ConfigMaps are left behind and need pruning, which GitOps tools do for you.
